subtopics.title: Interrupts & Interrupt Service Routines
subtopics.subtitle: Interrupt vs polling, interrupt classes, 8085/8086 interrupt pins and how an ISR is written

concepts.text: What Is an Interrupt?

An interrupt is a signal, from hardware or from software, that temporarily suspends the program the CPU is executing so that an urgent task can be handled. The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves enough information to come back later, and transfers control to a special subroutine called the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or interrupt handler. When the ISR finishes, the saved state is restored and the interrupted program continues exactly where it left off, unaware that anything happened.
Interrupts are the main way an I/O device tells the processor "I need attention now" without the processor having to keep checking. Examples are a key press, a timer tick, a completed serial byte, a power-failure warning, or a divide-by-zero error inside the CPU itself.

CPU runs other work; responds only when needed
Depends on how often the loop checks

concepts.text: Classification of Interrupts
Interrupts are grouped along several independent axes:
items: Hardware interrupts arrive on a physical pin of the processor from an external device (keyboard, timer, 8259 controller). Software interrupts are caused by executing an instruction such as INT n in 8086 or RST n in 8085; they are used as system calls (for example INT 21H for DOS services).

Maskable interrupts can be ignored (masked) by the program: 8085 RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 and INTR, 8086 INTR. Non-maskable interrupts cannot be disabled and are reserved for critical events such as power failure: 8085 TRAP, 8086 NMI.

Vectored interrupts jump to a fixed, predefined address (8085 TRAP and RST 7.5/6.5/5.5; every 8086 interrupt through its vector table). Non-vectored interrupts require the device to supply the address or an instruction code on the data bus (8085 INTR).
Internal interrupts (exceptions or traps) are generated by the CPU itself when an abnormal condition occurs during an instruction: divide-by-zero, overflow (INTO) or single-step mode in the 8086.

Edge-triggered inputs respond to a transition (8085 RST 7.5 latches a rising edge; 8086 NMI). Level-triggered inputs must be held active until the CPU samples them (8085 RST 6.5, RST 5.5, INTR; 8086 INTR).

concepts.text: 8085 Interrupts

rows: None: device supplies RST n or CALL

concepts.text: Controlling 8085 interrupts:
items: EI (Enable Interrupts) sets the interrupt-enable flip-flop; DI (Disable Interrupts) clears it. When any interrupt is accepted the 8085 automatically disables further interrupts, so an ISR must execute EI again before returning if nesting is wanted.

SIM (Set Interrupt Mask) writes the accumulator to the mask logic: bits 0, 1, 2 mask RST 5.5, 6.5, 7.5 (1 = masked); bit 3 (MSE) must be 1 for the mask bits to take effect; bit 4 resets the RST 7.5 latch. Bits 6 and 7 drive serial output SOD.
RIM (Read Interrupt Mask) loads the accumulator with the mask status, the pending status of RST 7.5/6.5/5.5, the interrupt-enable flag and the serial input SID.

INTR is acknowledged with INTA; the external logic must place an RST n (one byte) or CALL (three bytes) opcode on the data bus. The eight software RST n instructions vector to 8 × n: RST 0 → 0000H up to RST 7 → 0038H.
TRAP and the RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 inputs are vectored: their service routines begin at fixed locations only 8 bytes apart, so each location normally holds just a JMP to the real ISR.

concepts.plainText: RST n vectors to address 8 × n (RST 5 → 0028H, RST 7 → 0038H)

concepts.text: 8086 Interrupts
The 8086 has two interrupt pins and 256 possible interrupt types:
items: NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt): positive-edge-triggered, cannot be disabled, always type 2 (vector at 00008H). Used for memory parity error or power-failure warning.

INTR (Interrupt Request): level-triggered, maskable by the Interrupt Flag IF. When accepted, the 8086 runs two INTA (interrupt acknowledge) bus cycles and the interrupting device, usually an 8259 PIC, places the 8-bit type number on the data bus during the second cycle.
INT n: a 2-byte software interrupt instruction (opcode CDH followed by the type n); INT 3 has a special 1-byte opcode (CCH) for breakpoints. INTO interrupts (type 4) only if the Overflow flag is set.

Predefined internal types: 0 divide error (DIV/IDIV quotient too large or divisor zero), 1 single step (executed after every instruction while TF = 1), 2 NMI, 3 breakpoint, 4 overflow. Types 5 to 31 are reserved by Intel; types 32 to 255 are free for the user.

concepts.text: Structure of an Interrupt Service Routine

An ISR looks like a subroutine but is entered by hardware and must leave the machine exactly as it found it. The CPU saves the return address (and in the 8086 the flags) automatically; everything else that the ISR touches must be saved on the stack by the programmer. The typical order is: save registers, re-enable interrupts if nesting is allowed, service the device (read or write the data port, clear the request), send any end-of-interrupt command to the controller, restore registers, and return with IRET (8086) or EI followed by RET (8085).

KBD_ISR:  PUSH AX          ; save every register the ISR uses
          PUSH DX
          STI              ; allow higher-priority nesting (optional)
          MOV  DX, 0300H   ; data port of the device
          IN   AL, DX      ; read the byte, clears the request
          MOV  [BUF], AL   ; store it for the main program
          MOV  AL, 20H     ; non-specific EOI for the 8259
          OUT  20H, AL
          POP  DX          ; restore in reverse order
          POP  AX
          IRET             ; pops IP, CS and FLAGS
Enabling, Disabling, Nesting and Latency
Controlling and living with interrupts:
items: In the 8086 the Interrupt Flag IF controls INTR only: STI sets IF (enable), CLI clears IF (disable). NMI, software INT n and internal exceptions are never affected by IF. Accepting any interrupt clears IF and TF automatically, and IRET restores them from the saved flags.

Nested interrupts: if the ISR executes STI (8086) or EI (8085) early, a higher-priority request can interrupt the ISR itself. Each level pushes its own return information, so the stack must be large enough for the deepest nesting expected.

Interrupt latency is the delay between a request and the first ISR instruction: the CPU must complete the current instruction (worst case the longest one), push the return state and fetch the vector. Long instructions, CLI sections and higher-priority ISRs all add to it, so critical sections that disable interrupts must be kept short.
Because the 8085 saves only the program counter, an 8085 ISR must PUSH PSW to preserve the accumulator and flags; the 8086 saves FLAGS automatically but not the general registers.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: How the 8085 Decides to Accept an Interrupt

At the end of every instruction the 8085 checks its five inputs in priority order. TRAP is accepted whenever it is present, because it bypasses both the enable flip-flop and the masks. Each RST input is accepted only if three things are true together: the request is present (the pin level for RST 6.5 and 5.5, the internal latch for RST 7.5), its SIM mask bit is 0, and the interrupt-enable flip-flop is set. INTR has no mask bit, so it depends only on the pin and the enable flip-flop.

concepts.plainText: RST 6.5 is accepted only if IE = 1 AND M6.5 = 0 AND the RST 6.5 pin is high

rows: M7.5, M6.5, M5.5 as currently set

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: build a SIM byte and decode a RIM byte

Goal: unmask only RST 6.5 and discard any old RST 7.5 request
  SOD SDE -  R7.5 MSE M7.5 M6.5 M5.5
   0   0  0   1    1    1    0    1   = 0001 1101 = 1DH

RIM returns A = 3AH = 0011 1010
  SID=0  I7.5=0  I6.5=1  I5.5=1  IE=1  M7.5=0  M6.5=1  M5.5=0
  RST 6.5 is requested but masked, so it waits.
  RST 5.5 is requested, unmasked and IE = 1:
  it is accepted at the end of the current instruction (002CH).

ORG  0000H
        JMP  MAIN        ; reset starts execution at 0000H
        ORG  003CH
        JMP  ISR75       ; 3-byte JMP fits in 003CH-003FH
MAIN:   LXI  SP,2100H    ; stack must exist before EI
        MVI  A,0BH       ; MSE=1, unmask RST 7.5 only
        SIM
        EI
LOOP:   JMP  LOOP        ; main work goes here
ISR75:  PUSH PSW         ; CPU saved only PC: save A and flags
        IN   40H         ; read the device, removes its request
        STA  2050H       ; store the byte for the main program
        POP  PSW         ; restore A and flags
        EI               ; takes effect after RET
        RET

Why EI goes immediately before RET: the 8085 delays the enable by one instruction, so the RET always completes before a waiting request is accepted. If EI were placed earlier, a second request could enter the ISR again while it still had registers on the stack, and a steady stream of requests could make the stack grow without limit. Putting EI at the very start is correct only when nesting is actually wanted and the stack is large enough.

Worked example 2: latency and stack for RST 7.5 at 5 MHz

T = 1 / 5 MHz = 0.2 µs
Worst case: request arrives as an 18-T CALL starts
  finish CALL          18 T
  push PC, go to 003CH 12 T
  JMP ISR75 at 003CH   10 T
To the vector : (18 + 12) x 0.2 = 6 µs
To ISR75 itself: (18 + 12 + 10) x 0.2 = 8 µs

Stack (SP = 2100H, return address 0126H):
  20FFH <- 01H, 20FEH <- 26H, SP = 20FEH

concepts.plainText: Latency = number of T-states before the ISR starts / clock frequency

concepts.text: Common mistakes with 8085 interrupts:
items: Writing mask bits with MSE = 0: SIM then ignores D2-D0 and the masks stay as they were.
Reading a 1 in a mask bit as enabled: in both SIM and RIM a 1 means masked.
Expecting EI to unmask RST 7.5/6.5/5.5: EI only sets the global enable; masks come from SIM.
Forgetting that SDE (D6) must be 1 for D7 to reach the SOD pin.
Expecting a short pulse on RST 6.5 or RST 5.5 to be remembered: only RST 7.5 is latched.
Skipping PUSH PSW in an ISR: the 8085 saves only PC, so the interrupted program's A and flags would be corrupted.

concepts.text: For any SIM or RIM question, write the byte in binary first and label the eight bits (SIM: SOD SDE x R7.5 MSE M7.5 M6.5 M5.5; RIM: SID I7.5 I6.5 I5.5 IE M7.5 M6.5 M5.5). Most wrong options come from a missing MSE or SDE bit or from reading a mask bit backwards.

formulas.plainText: RST n vectors to address 8 × n
Latency = time to finish current instruction + save state + fetch vector

notes.text: Memorise the 8085 vector addresses as steps of 8 from TRAP: 0024H (TRAP), 002CH (RST 5.5), 0034H (RST 6.5), 003CH (RST 7.5). Priority order is the same as the address order: TRAP > RST 7.5 > RST 6.5 > RST 5.5 > INTR.
IF (STI/CLI) masks only INTR in the 8086. NMI, INT n and the internal exceptions are always accepted, and a question that says "CLI disables all interrupts" is wrong.

RST 7.5 is the only 8085 interrupt that is edge-triggered and latched: a short pulse is remembered until served or until SIM bit 4 clears it. RST 6.5 and 5.5 are level inputs and are lost if the device drops the line before the CPU samples it.
In the 8085, accepting any interrupt resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop. Forgetting EI before RET in an ISR is a classic bug: the first interrupt is served and every later one is ignored.

formulas.title: 8085 RST n vector
formulas.description: The eight 8085 software restart instructions jump to fixed addresses 8 bytes apart, from RST 0 at 0000H to RST 7 at 0038H.

formulas.title: 8085 hardware vectors
formulas.description: Vector addresses of the four vectored 8085 interrupts; each fractional RST vector lies midway between two integer RST vectors.

formulas.title: 8086 type-to-vector address
formulas.description: The 8086 finds the ISR for interrupt type n at memory address 4n in the interrupt vector table (NMI is type 2, so 00008H).

formulas.title: Interrupt latency
formulas.plainText: Latency = finish current instruction + save state + fetch vector
formulas.description: Delay between an interrupt request and the first ISR instruction; worst case includes the longest instruction and any interval during which interrupts are disabled.

flashcards.front: What is the main disadvantage of polling compared with interrupt-driven I/O?
flashcards.back: The CPU wastes time in a loop repeatedly reading device status even when no device needs service, whereas an interrupt lets the CPU do useful work and respond only when a device signals.

flashcards.front: List the 8085 interrupts in order of priority with their vector addresses.
flashcards.back: TRAP (0024H) > RST 7.5 (003CH) > RST 6.5 (0034H) > RST 5.5 (002CH) > INTR (non-vectored, address supplied by the device).

flashcards.front: Which 8086 interrupts are NOT affected by the CLI instruction?
flashcards.back: NMI, software interrupts (INT n, INTO) and internal exceptions such as divide error and single step. CLI clears IF, which masks only the INTR pin.

flashcards.front: What do the 8085 instructions SIM and RIM do?
flashcards.back: SIM writes the accumulator to set or clear the masks of RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 (with MSE bit 3 = 1) and can reset the RST 7.5 latch; RIM reads the mask bits, pending interrupts and the interrupt-enable status into the accumulator.

questions.questionText: The vector address of the 8085 interrupt RST 6.5 is:
questions.explanation: The vectored 8085 interrupts are 8 bytes apart: TRAP 0024H, RST 5.5 002CH, RST 6.5 0034H and RST 7.5 003CH. RST 6.5 lies midway between RST 6 (0030H) and RST 7 (0038H), that is 6.5 × 8 = 52 = 0034H.

questions.questionText: In polling (programmed) I/O, how does the CPU find out that a device needs service?
options: The device drives an interrupt pin and the CPU jumps to a vector address
The device takes over the system bus and writes directly into memory
The CPU executes a software interrupt instruction that asks the device for its status
It repeatedly reads the device status register in a loop until the ready bit is set
questions.explanation: Polling is CPU-initiated: the program keeps testing a status bit. An interrupt pin is interrupt-driven I/O and taking over the bus is DMA.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 interrupt input is non-vectored?
questions.explanation: TRAP and RST 7.5/6.5/5.5 branch to fixed internal addresses. For INTR the external logic must supply an RST n or CALL instruction on the data bus during INTA.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 interrupt input is purely edge-triggered, with the request stored in an internal flip-flop?
questions.explanation: RST 7.5 responds to a rising edge and latches it. RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR are level-sensitive; TRAP needs both an edge and a sustained high level.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a software interrupt in the 8085?
options: A rising edge on the RST 7.5 pin
A high level on the TRAP pin
A request on INTR answered with INTA
questions.explanation: A software interrupt is caused by an instruction in the program; RST 3 is an instruction that pushes PC and branches to 0018H. The other three are hardware requests arriving on pins.

questions.questionText: What does the 8085 instruction EI do?
options: Enables TRAP, which is disabled after every reset
Sets the interrupt-enable flip-flop so that the maskable interrupts can be accepted
Clears the RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 mask bits
questions.explanation: EI only sets the global interrupt-enable flip-flop. The individual mask bits are changed only by SIM, and TRAP is never disabled, so it needs no enabling.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 instruction disables all maskable interrupts in one step?
questions.explanation: DI resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop, blocking RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5 and INTR (TRAP is unaffected). CLI is the 8086 equivalent and does not exist in the 8085 instruction set.

questions.questionText: The 8085 software instruction RST 5 transfers control to address:
questions.explanation: RST n branches to 8 × n: 8 × 5 = 40 = 0028H. 002CH is the hardware RST 5.5 vector, and 0050H results from multiplying by 16 instead of 8.

questions.questionText: An 8085 interrupt service routine that must allow later maskable interrupts to be accepted should normally end with:
questions.explanation: The 8085 disables interrupts automatically when it accepts one, so the ISR must re-enable them with EI and then return with an ordinary RET. The 8085 has no IRET instruction.

questions.questionText: An interrupt is described as maskable when:
options: It always has the highest priority in the system
Its service routine starts at a fixed address
It is generated by an instruction rather than by a pin
The program can disable it so that a request on it is ignored
questions.explanation: Maskable means it can be turned off by software (EI/DI, SIM, STI/CLI). A fixed address describes a vectored interrupt and an instruction-generated one is a software interrupt.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 interrupt has the lowest priority?
questions.explanation: The priority order is TRAP > RST 7.5 > RST 6.5 > RST 5.5 > INTR, so INTR is served last when several requests are pending together.

questions.questionText: In the 8086, the instruction STI:
options: Sets TF so that the processor single-steps
Enables the NMI input, which is disabled after reset
Sets IF so that requests on the INTR pin are recognised
Stores the interrupt vector of the current ISR in the vector table
questions.explanation: STI sets the Interrupt Flag; IF affects only the maskable INTR input. NMI cannot be disabled, and TF is the Trap Flag used for single-stepping.

questions.questionText: What does the 8085 instruction RIM do?
options: Writes the accumulator into the interrupt mask register
Loads HL with the vector address of the highest-priority pending interrupt
Returns from an interrupt service routine and re-enables interrupts
Loads the accumulator with the mask bits, pending-interrupt bits, the interrupt-enable status and the SID bit
questions.explanation: RIM (Read Interrupt Mask) is the read side: D7 = SID, D6-D4 = pending 7.5/6.5/5.5, D3 = IE, D2-D0 = masks. Writing the masks is SIM.

questions.questionText: How many interrupt input pins does the 8085 have?
questions.explanation: The inputs are TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR. INTA is an output (acknowledge), not an interrupt input.

questions.questionText: When the 8085 accepts a request on INTR, which signal does it activate so that the external logic can supply an instruction?
questions.explanation: INTA is the interrupt acknowledge output. The device or controller places an RST n or CALL opcode on the data bus while INTA is low. HLDA acknowledges a DMA HOLD request.

questions.questionText: An 8085 program must unmask RST 7.5, mask RST 6.5 and RST 5.5, leave the RST 7.5 latch alone and not use SOD. The byte loaded into A before SIM is:
questions.explanation: SIM bits: D3 MSE = 1 to make the masks valid, D2 M7.5 = 0, D1 M6.5 = 1, D0 M5.5 = 1, all others 0: 0000 1011 = 0BH. 03H forgets MSE, so the masks would not change.

questions.questionText: An 8085 executes MVI A,0DH followed by SIM. Which of RST 7.5, RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are now unmasked?
questions.explanation: 0DH = 0000 1101: MSE (D3) = 1 so the masks load; M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 0, M5.5 = 1. A 1 means masked, so only RST 6.5 is unmasked.

questions.questionText: What is the effect of MVI A,1FH followed by SIM in an 8085?
options: RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all masked and any pending RST 7.5 request is cleared
RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all unmasked and any pending RST 7.5 request is cleared
RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all masked and SOD is set to 1
Nothing changes, because the mask-set-enable bit is 0
questions.explanation: 1FH = 0001 1111: D4 = 1 resets the RST 7.5 flip-flop, D3 MSE = 1 enables loading, and D2-D0 = 111 mask all three. D6 SDE = 0, so SOD is not affected.

questions.questionText: An 8085 has RST 6.5 masked. The program executes MVI A,05H then SIM, intending to unmask RST 6.5. What happens?
options: RST 6.5 is unmasked and RST 7.5 and RST 5.5 are masked
All three RST inputs are unmasked
RST 6.5 is unmasked and SOD outputs 1
The masks do not change, because bit D3 (MSE) of 05H is 0
questions.explanation: 05H = 0000 0101 has MSE = 0, so SIM ignores D2-D0 and the old masks remain. The correct byte would be 0DH (MSE = 1, M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 0, M5.5 = 1).

questions.questionText: In an 8085, RIM returns A = 62H. Which statement is correct?
options: RST 7.5 and RST 6.5 are pending and the interrupt system is disabled
RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are pending and the interrupt system is enabled
RST 7.5 and RST 6.5 are pending and the interrupt system is enabled
Only RST 6.5 is pending and RST 5.5 is masked

questions.questionText: Which byte, used with SIM, sends a logic 1 out of the 8085 SOD pin without changing the interrupt masks?
questions.explanation: SOD = D7 = 1 and SDE = D6 = 1 (serial data enable), with MSE = D3 = 0 so the masks are untouched: 1100 0000 = C0H. 80H lacks SDE, 40H outputs 0, and C8H would also load the masks (all unmasked).

questions.questionText: The one-byte opcode of the 8085 instruction RST 5 is:
questions.explanation: RST n is encoded 11 NNN 111. For n = 5 (101): 1110 1111 = EFH. E7H is RST 4, 28H is the vector address rather than the opcode, and F5H is PUSH PSW.

questions.questionText: When an 8085 acknowledges an INTR request, what must the external hardware place on the data bus?
options: An 8-bit type number that the CPU multiplies by 4
An RST n opcode or the three bytes of a CALL instruction
The 16-bit ISR address alone, with no opcode
Nothing, because the CPU then jumps to 0024H
questions.explanation: INTR is non-vectored, so during INTA the CPU fetches an instruction from the data bus: a one-byte RST n or a CALL (with further INTA cycles for its two address bytes). The type-number method belongs to the 8086.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the 8085 TRAP interrupt is correct?
options: It is both edge- and level-sensitive and cannot be disabled by DI or SIM
It can be masked by setting bit D3 of the SIM byte
It is non-vectored, so the device supplies the ISR address
It has the lowest priority of the five interrupt inputs
questions.explanation: TRAP needs a rising edge followed by a sustained high level, which protects it against noise. It is non-maskable, vectored to 0024H and has the highest priority.

questions.questionText: An interrupt is called vectored when:
options: The interrupting device must supply the ISR address or an opcode on the data bus
The processor itself knows the starting address of its service routine
It can be disabled by the program
It is triggered by an edge rather than a level
questions.explanation: For a vectored interrupt the ISR address is fixed or looked up internally (8085 TRAP, RST 7.5/6.5/5.5; every 8086 type through the IVT). If the device must supply it, the interrupt is non-vectored, like 8085 INTR.

questions.questionText: Which list gives the 8085 hardware interrupts in decreasing order of priority?
questions.explanation: TRAP is highest, then RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, and INTR is lowest. Among the three RST inputs, the higher the RST number (and vector address), the higher the priority; TRAP is the exception, with the lowest vector (0024H) but the highest priority.

questions.questionText: The RST 5.5 vector is 002CH and the next restart vector, RST 6, is at 0030H. How many bytes are available at 002CH before RST 6 begins?
questions.explanation: 0030H − 002CH = 4 bytes. That is too small for a real ISR, so the location normally holds a 3-byte JMP to the routine elsewhere in memory.

questions.questionText: An 8085 ISR modifies the accumulator and the flags. Which instruction at the start of the ISR preserves both?
questions.explanation: PUSH PSW saves the accumulator and the flag register as one 16-bit pair. PUSH A does not exist, PUSHF is an 8086 instruction and SPHL copies HL into SP.

questions.questionText: Interrupt latency is best defined as:
options: The time from the interrupt request until the first instruction of the ISR begins
The total time spent executing the ISR
The time from the end of the ISR until the main program resumes
The number of interrupts the CPU can service per second
questions.explanation: Latency covers finishing the current instruction, saving the return state and fetching the vector. The ISR execution time is a separate figure, the service time.

questions.questionText: Which statement about software interrupts is correct?
options: In the 8086 they are blocked by CLI
They occur exactly where the interrupt instruction is placed, so they are synchronous with the program
They need an interrupt acknowledge bus cycle to obtain the type
They are triggered by a signal from an external device
questions.explanation: INT n (8086) and RST n (8085) are instructions, so they happen at a predictable point. The type is in the instruction, no INTA cycle is needed, and IF does not block them.

questions.questionText: An 8085 ISR ends with EI immediately followed by RET, and another interrupt is already pending. Why is the ISR not interrupted before RET executes?
options: RET cannot be interrupted because it is a privileged instruction
The pending request is discarded when EI is executed
EI takes effect only after two further instructions have been executed
EI takes effect only after the instruction that follows it has been executed
questions.explanation: The 8085 delays the enable by one instruction, so RET completes and the stack is unwound before the next interrupt is accepted. This keeps the stack from growing with every back-to-back request.

questions.questionText: An 8085 ISR for RST 6.5 ends with RET but the programmer forgot EI. What is the result?
options: Later RST 7.5, 6.5, 5.5 and INTR requests are ignored, but TRAP is still accepted
All interrupts including TRAP are ignored
The next RST 6.5 request re-enables interrupts automatically
The RET fails and the program restarts at 0000H
questions.explanation: Accepting an interrupt resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop. Without EI it stays reset, so every maskable request is ignored; only the non-maskable TRAP still gets through.

questions.questionText: An 8085 executes HLT with interrupts enabled. How can it continue executing instructions?
options: Only through RESET, because interrupts are not sampled in the halt state
Only through TRAP, because maskable interrupts are disabled by HLT
Through an enabled interrupt (or TRAP), or through RESET
Only through a HOLD request, which restarts the program after the DMA transfer
questions.explanation: In the halt state the 8085 still samples its interrupt pins; a valid interrupt pushes PC and enters the ISR, returning to the instruction after HLT. RESET also ends the halt. HOLD only lends the bus and the CPU stays halted.

questions.questionText: A CPU polls a device every 100 µs and each poll takes 4 µs, whether or not the device is ready. What fraction of CPU time is spent polling?
questions.explanation: Fraction = poll time / polling period = 4 µs / 100 µs = 0.04 = 4%. This time is lost even when the device has nothing to transfer.

questions.questionText: Which of the following increases the worst-case interrupt latency of a system?
options: Using a vectored interrupt instead of a non-vectored one
Making the ISR of that interrupt shorter
Long sections of code that run with interrupts disabled
Giving the interrupt a higher priority
questions.explanation: A request that arrives while interrupts are disabled must wait for the matching EI/STI, so disabled sections add directly to latency. The other three either reduce latency or do not affect it.

questions.questionText: What is the effect of MVI A,18H followed by SIM in an 8085?
options: Any pending RST 7.5 request is cleared and RST 7.5, 6.5 and 5.5 are all unmasked
Only RST 7.5 is unmasked and its latch is cleared
All three are masked and the pending RST 7.5 request is cleared
SOD outputs 1 and the masks stay as they were
questions.explanation: 18H = 0001 1000: D4 = 1 resets the RST 7.5 flip-flop, D3 MSE = 1 loads the masks, and D2-D0 = 000 unmask all three. D7 and D6 are 0, so SOD is unaffected.

questions.questionText: The TRAP vector 0024H is sometimes called "RST 4.5". Using the rule vector = 8 × n, what value of n gives 0024H?
questions.explanation: 0024H = 36 decimal, and 36 / 8 = 4.5. Reading 24 as decimal gives 3, and dividing 24H by 16 gives 2.25. The same reasoning gives 5.5, 6.5 and 7.5 for 002CH, 0034H and 003CH.

questions.questionText: Which 8085 interrupts are controlled by the mask bits written with SIM?
questions.explanation: SIM has mask bits only for the three RST inputs. INTR is controlled only by EI/DI, and TRAP cannot be masked at all.

questions.questionText: An 8085 main loop executes RIM and gets A = 2BH. RST 6.5 is being requested but is not being serviced. Why?
options: A pending RST 7.5 request of higher priority is being served first
RST 6.5 is edge-triggered and the edge was missed
questions.explanation: 2BH = 0010 1011: D5 I6.5 = 1 (pending), D3 IE = 1 (enabled), D6 I7.5 = 0, and D1 M6.5 = 1, so the request is masked. RST 6.5 is level-triggered.

questions.questionText: In an 8085, RST 7.5 and RST 5.5 are both unmasked but interrupts are disabled with DI. A 1 µs pulse arrives on each pin, after which both pins stay low. The program later executes EI. Which interrupt is serviced?
options: Both, RST 7.5 first and then RST 5.5
Neither, because both requests arrived while interrupts were disabled
questions.explanation: The rising edge on RST 7.5 sets its internal flip-flop, which holds the request until it is served. RST 5.5 is level-sensitive and not latched, so its request vanished when the pin went low.

questions.questionText: A keyboard is pressed 10 times per second. Polling checks it 500 times per second at 20 µs per check. With interrupts, each key press costs 50 µs (entry, service and return). How many times more CPU time does polling use than the interrupt method?
questions.explanation: Polling: 500 × 20 µs = 10000 µs per second. Interrupts: 10 × 50 µs = 500 µs per second. Ratio = 10000 / 500 = 20.

questions.questionText: An 8085 runs at a 3 MHz clock. A RST 7.5 request arrives just as an 18 T-state CALL instruction begins, and the CPU then needs 12 T-states to save PC and branch to 003CH. What is the worst-case latency until the vector location is fetched?
questions.explanation: T = 1 / 3 MHz = 0.333 µs. Latency = (18 + 12) T-states × 0.333 µs = 30 / 3 = 10 µs. Counting only the CALL gives 6 µs and only the response 4 µs.

questions.questionText: An 8085 executes MVI A,0EH, SIM, EI. Then a rising edge arrives on RST 7.5 while RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are both held high. Which interrupt is serviced first, and at which vector?
options: None, because all three are masked
questions.explanation: 0EH = 0000 1110: MSE = 1, M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 1, M5.5 = 0. RST 7.5 and RST 6.5 are masked despite their higher priority, so RST 5.5 is the only one accepted, at 002CH.

questions.questionText: During INTA, the interrupting device places DFH on the 8085 data bus. Where does the processor transfer control?
questions.explanation: DFH = 11 011 111, the RST n pattern 11 NNN 111 with NNN = 011, so it is RST 3. The vector is 8 × 3 = 24 = 0018H. 0030H results from multiplying by 16.

questions.questionText: An 8085 has SP = 2000H. The 3-byte instruction LXI H,3000H occupies 2050H-2052H, and a RST 6.5 request is accepted at its end. After the return address is pushed, what do locations 1FFFH and 1FFEH contain?
questions.explanation: The return address is the next instruction, 2050H + 3 = 2053H. A push decrements SP and stores the high byte first: 20H goes to 1FFFH and 53H to 1FFEH, leaving SP = 1FFEH.

questions.questionText: An 8085 program runs RIM, ANI x, CPI x and JZ to jump only when RST 7.5 is pending AND the interrupt system is enabled. What is x?
questions.explanation: In the RIM byte, D6 = RST 7.5 pending and D3 = IE, so x = 0100 1000 = 48H. 44H picks D2 (the RST 7.5 mask) instead of IE, and 84H picks the SID bit.

questions.questionText: With a single SIM, an 8085 must mask RST 7.5 and RST 5.5, unmask RST 6.5, clear the RST 7.5 latch and output 0 on SOD. The byte in A is:
questions.explanation: SOD = 0, SDE = 1, D5 = 0, R7.5 = 1, MSE = 1, M7.5 = 1, M6.5 = 0, M5.5 = 1: 0101 1101 = 5DH. 1DH leaves SDE = 0 so SOD is not driven, DDH outputs 1, and 5AH inverts the mask bits.

subtopics.title: Interrupt Processing, Vector Table & the 8259 PIC
subtopics.subtitle: 8086 interrupt response step by step, IVT address arithmetic, priorities and the 8259

concepts.text: Interrupt Processing Sequence in the 8086
When an interrupt of type n is recognised, the 8086 performs these steps in hardware:
items: 1. Complete the instruction currently being executed (an interrupt is never taken in the middle of an instruction, except that string instructions with REP can be interrupted between repetitions).
2. Push the FLAGS register onto the stack (SP = SP − 2).
3. Clear IF and TF so that the ISR starts with INTR masked and single-stepping off.
4. Push CS, then push IP, so the full return address is saved (SP is now 6 lower than before).
5. Read the new IP from memory address 4n and the new CS from address 4n + 2 of the Interrupt Vector Table.
6. Execute the ISR at the new CS:IP.
7. The ISR ends with IRET, which pops IP, CS and FLAGS in that order, restoring IF and TF as they were and resuming the interrupted program.

concepts.text:
For an external INTR request an extra step precedes the sequence: the 8086 checks IF at the end of the instruction and, if it is set, runs two INTA bus cycles to obtain the type number from the interrupting device. For NMI the type is fixed at 2, and for INT n or an internal exception the type is known from the instruction or the condition, so no acknowledge cycle is needed.
The 8085 is simpler: it pushes only the 16-bit program counter, resets the interrupt-enable flip-flop, jumps to the vector address and returns with an ordinary RET. Flags and registers are not saved automatically, so the ISR must PUSH PSW and PUSH the register pairs it uses.
The 8086 Interrupt Vector Table

The Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) occupies the lowest 1 KB of memory, from 00000H to 003FFH. It holds 256 entries, one for each interrupt type 0 to 255, and every entry is a 4-byte far pointer to an ISR: the low word is the offset (IP) and the high word is the segment (CS). Because each entry is 4 bytes, the entry for type n starts at physical address 4 × n.

concepts.plainText: Vector address of type n = 4 × n

concepts.text: Worked example: INT 21H.
items: Type = 21H = 33 decimal, so the entry starts at 4 × 33 = 132 = 00084H.
Memory 00084H and 00085H hold the ISR offset (low byte first); 00086H and 00087H hold the ISR segment.
If the four bytes are 10 00 00 F0 (in address order), the ISR is at CS:IP = F000H:0010H, physical address F0000H + 0010H = F0010H.
Going the other way: a vector found at 00034H belongs to type 34H ÷ 4 = 0DH = 13.

rows: DIV or IDIV with a zero divisor or a quotient too large for AL/AX
Taken after every instruction while the Trap Flag TF = 1 (debuggers)
Rising edge on the NMI pin; cannot be masked
One-byte INT 3 instruction (CCH) inserted by debuggers
INTO instruction executed while the Overflow flag OF = 1

concepts.text: Priority of 8086 Interrupts

rows: Taken only after the other pending interrupts

concepts.text: The 8259 Programmable Interrupt Controller
The CPU only ranks its own few inputs; priority among many external devices is decided by the 8259A, a 28-pin controller that funnels their requests into the single INTR pin of the 8085/8086:
items: Eight interrupt request inputs IR0 to IR7, each edge- or level-triggered as programmed. One master with up to eight slaves on its IR inputs (linked by the CAS0-CAS2 cascade lines and the SP/EN pin) handles 64 interrupt sources.

Interrupt Request Register (IRR): one bit per input, set when a request arrives. Interrupt Mask Register (IMR): a 1 bit masks (ignores) the corresponding input. In-Service Register (ISR): the bit of the request currently being serviced, so lower-priority requests are held off until an EOI.
Priority resolver: chooses the highest-priority unmasked request in IRR, sets its ISR bit and raises INT to the CPU.

Type number generation: the upper five bits of the vector type come from ICW2 and the lower three bits are the IR level, so with ICW2 = 08H the inputs IR0-IR7 produce types 08H-0FH (the PC convention: IR0 = timer at type 8, IR1 = keyboard at type 9).

End of Interrupt (EOI): the ISR must tell the 8259 when it is done by writing OCW2 (20H is a non-specific EOI that clears the highest ISR bit); otherwise no equal- or lower-priority interrupt is ever passed on. Automatic EOI mode clears the bit on the second INTA instead.

rows: Edge/level trigger, single or cascade, whether ICW4 follows
Upper 5 bits of the interrupt type (T7-T3) for 8086 mode
Master: which IR lines have slaves; slave: its ID 0-7
8086/8085 mode, auto EOI, buffered mode, special fully nested mode
Read IRR or ISR, poll mode, special mask mode

concepts.text: 8259 with the 8086, the INTA handshake step by step:
items: A device pulls an IR input; the 8259 sets the IRR bit, resolves priority against the ISR and IMR, and asserts INT (wired to INTR of the 8086).

If IF = 1 the 8086 finishes the current instruction and issues the first INTA pulse: the 8259 freezes the request, sets the ISR bit for the winning input and clears its IRR bit. Nothing is placed on the bus yet.

On the second INTA pulse the 8259 drives the 8-bit type number onto D0-D7 (AD0-AD7). The 8086 multiplies it by 4, reads the vector and enters the ISR. In cascade mode the master uses CAS0-CAS2 to tell the responsible slave to supply the type.
The ISR services the device and writes an EOI to the 8259 before IRET, clearing the ISR bit so that equal- and lower-priority requests can be recognised again.

concepts.text: Interrupt priority schemes: several general techniques decide which of several simultaneous requests is served first.
items: Fixed priority: each line has a permanent rank (the 8259 default, called fully nested mode, gives IR0 the highest and IR7 the lowest priority). Simple, but a busy high-priority device can starve the others.
Rotating priority: after an input is served it becomes the lowest priority, so every device gets a fair turn (8259 automatic or specific rotation set through OCW2).

Polled (software) priority: on a single interrupt the CPU reads the status of each device in a fixed order; the order of polling is the priority. Cheap in hardware, slow in response. The 8259 supports a poll mode through OCW3 in which the CPU reads the highest pending request instead of using INTA.

Daisy chain (hardware): the INTA signal passes from device to device along a chain; the first device with a pending request blocks the acknowledge from travelling further and puts its vector on the bus, so the device closest to the CPU has the highest priority.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: IVT Arithmetic and Programming the 8259

Multiplying the type by 4 is the same as shifting it left two places, so the 8086 can form the IVT address with no arithmetic unit at all: type 60H (0110 0000) becomes 01 1000 0000 = 180H. Going backwards, the low two bits of any IVT entry address are always 00, so an address like 00086H is not the start of an entry but the third byte (address 4n + 2, the low byte of CS) of the type 21H entry. Remember that each entry is itself a far pointer, so after reading it the CPU still has to form CS × 16 + IP to reach the routine.

Worked example 1: INT 60H executed at CS:IP = 1200H:0343H
SS = 4000H, SP = 0100H; IVT bytes at 00180H: 80 00 00 24

Return IP = 0343H + 2 (INT n is 2 bytes) = 0345H
push FLAGS -> SS:00FEH = 400FEH   (then IF = 0, TF = 0)
push CS    -> SS:00FCH = 400FCH   (1200H)
push IP    -> SS:00FAH = 400FAH   (0345H), SP = 00FAH
Entry = 4 x 60H = 00180H
IP = 0080H, CS = 2400H -> ISR at 24000H + 0080H = 24080H
IRET later pops IP = 0345H, CS = 1200H, FLAGS; SP = 0100H

CLI                      ; no interrupt while the vector is half written
        XOR  AX, AX
        MOV  ES, AX              ; ES = 0000H, the IVT segment
        MOV  WORD PTR ES:[0180H], OFFSET MY_ISR  ; 4 x 60H = 180H: IP
        MOV  WORD PTR ES:[0182H], SEG MY_ISR     ; 182H: CS
        STI
        INT  60H                 ; test call: pushes FLAGS, CS, IP
        ; ...
MY_ISR: PUSH AX                  ; save what the ISR uses
        ; service the request
        POP  AX
        IRET                     ; pops IP, CS, FLAGS

rows: Rotate on specific EOI (L becomes lowest)
Set / clear rotate in AEOI mode

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: master at 20H/21H, one slave on master IR2
Slave at A0H/A1H, 8086 mode, edge-triggered

            Master                Slave
ICW1 (A0=0) 0001 0001 = 11H       11H  (cascade, ICW4 needed)
ICW2 (A0=1) 08H -> types 08H-0FH  70H -> types 70H-77H
ICW3 (A0=1) 0000 0100 = 04H       02H  (slave ID = 2)
ICW4 (A0=1) 0001 0001 = 11H       01H  (SFNM only on master)

Inputs available = 7 (master) + 8 (slave) = 15
Slave IR3 -> type 70H + 3 = 73H -> IVT entry 4 x 73H = 001CCH

concepts.plainText: Inputs with s slaves = (8 − s) + 8s = 8 + 7s, so 8 slaves give 64

concepts.text: Rotation keeps a busy device from starving the others. In automatic rotation, the level that has just been served becomes the lowest, so after IR3 the order is IR4, IR5, IR6, IR7, IR0, IR1, IR2, IR3. The set-priority command does the same job on demand: it names the level that must become lowest, and the one after it becomes highest. Both are OCW2 commands and can be issued at any time after initialisation.
Common mistakes in IVT and 8259 questions:
items: Writing 4 × type in decimal and reading the result as hex: 4 × 08H is 32 = 20H, not 32H.
Swapping the halves of an IVT entry: the offset (IP) is at 4n, the segment (CS) at 4n + 2.
Using the bit-mask form for a slave ICW3: the master gets one bit per slave, a slave gets its 3-bit ID.
Reading 1 in the IMR as enabled: a 1 in OCW1 masks that input.
Counting 8 inputs per chip in a cascade: each slave uses up one master input, so the total is 8 + 7s.
Forgetting D4 = 1 in ICW1 or D3 = 1 in OCW3, which turns the byte into a different command.

concepts.text: ICW2 is not an address. It gives the upper five bits of the type number; the 8086 then multiplies the type by 4 to find the IVT entry. With ICW2 = 08H, IR1 is type 09H and its vector is at 00024H, not at 00009H or 00008H.

formulas.plainText: IP is read from address 4n, CS from address 4n + 2
FLAGS + CS + IP = 6 bytes pushed per 8086 interrupt
Max IR lines = 8 × 8 = 64 with one master and eight slave 8259s
Type = ICW2 base (multiple of 8) + IR level

notes.text: Address questions are pure arithmetic: multiply the type by 4 (or shift left two bits). INT 21H → 21H × 4 = 84H, INT 10H → 40H, INT 80H → 200H. Given an address, divide by 4 to recover the type.

Order matters: the 8086 pushes FLAGS first, then CS, then IP; IRET pops IP, CS, FLAGS. In the IVT the low word (offset/IP) comes first and the high word (segment/CS) second, exactly like any far pointer.

IRR, ISR and IMR are the three 8259 registers MCQs confuse. IRR = requests waiting, ISR = request being served, IMR = requests deliberately ignored. IRR and ISR are read via OCW3; IMR is written via OCW1.
An 8259 ISR that forgets to send EOI still returns normally, but the ISR bit stays set and the controller will never again pass a request of that or lower priority to the CPU.

formulas.title: IVT vector address
formulas.description: Physical address of the 4-byte entry for interrupt type n in the 8086 interrupt vector table, which spans 00000H to 003FFH.

formulas.title: IVT entry layout
formulas.plainText: IP from address 4n, CS from address 4n + 2
formulas.description: Each entry stores the ISR offset in the low word and its segment in the high word; the 8086 loads both to reach the ISR.

formulas.title: IVT size
formulas.description: Total size of the interrupt vector table: 256 types, 4 bytes each.

formulas.title: Stack used per 8086 interrupt
formulas.description: Three words are pushed when an interrupt is accepted, so nesting k levels needs at least 6k bytes plus whatever each ISR pushes.

formulas.title: 8259 cascade capacity
formulas.description: Each of the master 8259 IR inputs can be fed by a slave 8259 with 8 inputs, giving 64 sources from nine controllers.

flashcards.front: What does the 8086 push on the stack when it accepts an interrupt, and in what order?
flashcards.back: FLAGS first, then CS, then IP (6 bytes in total). It then clears IF and TF and loads CS:IP from the vector table.

flashcards.front: Where is the vector for INT 21H stored and what do the four bytes contain?
flashcards.back: At 21H × 4 = 00084H. Bytes 00084H-00085H hold the ISR offset (IP) and 00086H-00087H hold the segment (CS).

flashcards.front: Name the three main registers of the 8259 PIC.
flashcards.back: IRR (Interrupt Request Register: pending requests), ISR (In-Service Register: request currently being served) and IMR (Interrupt Mask Register: masked inputs).

flashcards.front: What happens during the two INTA cycles between the 8086 and the 8259?
flashcards.back: First INTA: the 8259 resolves priority, sets the ISR bit and clears the IRR bit. Second INTA: the 8259 places the 8-bit interrupt type on the data bus for the CPU.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system the interrupt vector for INT 21H is stored starting at physical address:
questions.explanation: Each IVT entry is 4 bytes, so type n starts at 4 × n. 21H = 33 decimal, 4 × 33 = 132 = 00084H; the offset is at 00084H-00085H and the segment at 00086H-00087H.

questions.questionText: The number of 8259A controllers required to handle 64 hardware interrupt lines in cascade mode is:
questions.explanation: One master provides 8 IR inputs, and each input can be driven by a slave 8259A with its own 8 inputs: 8 slaves × 8 = 64 lines, requiring 8 slaves + 1 master = 9 controllers.

questions.questionText: When the 8086 accepts an interrupt, the stack pointer decreases by:
questions.explanation: The processor pushes three 16-bit words, FLAGS, CS and IP, so SP is reduced by 3 × 2 = 6 bytes. IRET pops the same three words in the reverse order.

questions.questionText: In the 8086, the Interrupt Vector Table occupies the physical address range:
questions.explanation: 256 types × 4 bytes = 1024 bytes = 1 KB at the bottom of memory: 00000H to 003FFH. 000FFH would allow only 1 byte per type.

questions.questionText: How many different interrupt types can the 8086 vector table hold?
questions.explanation: The type number is 8 bits, so there are 2^8 = 256 types (0 to 255), each with a 4-byte entry. 1024 is the size of the table in bytes, not the number of types.

questions.questionText: The 8086 NMI input is always serviced as interrupt type:
questions.explanation: NMI has the fixed type 2, so its vector is at 4 × 2 = 00008H. Type 0 is divide error, type 1 single step and type 4 overflow.

questions.questionText: The 8086 automatically generates a type 1 (single-step) interrupt:
options: Whenever DF = 1 during a string instruction
questions.explanation: The Trap Flag TF puts the 8086 in single-step mode, used by debuggers to run one instruction at a time. IF controls INTR, DF is the string direction and DIV overflow gives type 0.

questions.questionText: What makes the 8086 INT 3 instruction special?
options: It is the only non-maskable software interrupt
It is the instruction that turns on single-step mode
It is the only interrupt that does not push the flags
It has a one-byte opcode (CCH), convenient for inserting breakpoints
questions.explanation: Every other INT n is two bytes (CDH, n). A one-byte INT 3 can replace the first byte of any instruction, which is how debuggers plant breakpoints. All interrupts push FLAGS.

questions.questionText: The 8086 INTO instruction causes:
options: A type 4 interrupt every time it executes
A type 4 interrupt, but only if OF = 1
questions.explanation: INTO (interrupt on overflow, opcode CEH) tests the Overflow flag; if OF = 1 it calls type 4 through vector 00010H, otherwise it does nothing.

questions.questionText: The 8086 IRET instruction pops the stack in which order?
questions.explanation: The interrupt pushed FLAGS, CS and IP in that order, so IRET pops them in the reverse order: IP, CS, FLAGS. Restoring FLAGS also restores IF and TF.

questions.questionText: Which 8259 register is written with OCW1 to disable individual IR inputs?
questions.explanation: OCW1 is loaded into the IMR; a 1 bit masks the matching IR input. IRR holds waiting requests and ISR holds the levels being serviced.

questions.questionText: In the 8259, which register holds the interrupt requests that are waiting to be serviced?
questions.explanation: An IR input sets its IRR bit. When the request wins priority and is acknowledged, its IRR bit is cleared and the ISR bit is set.

questions.questionText: How many interrupt request inputs does a single 8259A provide?
questions.explanation: IR0 to IR7. Cascading one master with eight slaves raises the total to 64, but each chip still has 8 inputs.

questions.questionText: The OCW2 byte for a non-specific End of Interrupt command to the 8259 is:
questions.explanation: OCW2 = R SL EOI 0 0 L2 L1 L0. Non-specific EOI is R = 0, SL = 0, EOI = 1: 0010 0000 = 20H. 60H is a specific EOI for IR0, A0H rotates on non-specific EOI, 0AH is an OCW3 command.

questions.questionText: In the 8259 default fully nested mode, the priorities of the IR inputs are:
options: All equal, served in arrival order
questions.explanation: After initialisation the 8259 is in fully nested mode with fixed priority IR0 > IR1 > ... > IR7. Rotation has to be selected explicitly with OCW2.

questions.questionText: Which 8086 interrupt types are reserved by Intel for future use?
questions.explanation: Types 0-4 are dedicated (divide error, single step, NMI, breakpoint, overflow), 5-31 are reserved by Intel, and 32-255 are available to users.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 IVT entry, the first two bytes (at the lower address) hold:
options: The segment (CS) of the ISR, low byte first
The offset (IP) of the ISR, low byte first
questions.explanation: An IVT entry is a far pointer: bytes 4n and 4n + 1 hold IP, bytes 4n + 2 and 4n + 3 hold CS, each word stored little-endian.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system, the vector for INT 08H starts at physical address:
questions.explanation: Vector address = 4 × type = 4 × 08H = 20H = 00020H. 00032H comes from writing the decimal result 32 as if it were hex, and 00080H from multiplying by 16.

questions.questionText: An 8086 IVT entry begins at physical address 000A0H. Which interrupt type does it belong to?
questions.explanation: Type = address / 4 = A0H / 4 = 160 / 4 = 40 = 28H. Dividing by 2 gives 50H and dividing by 16 gives 0AH.

questions.questionText: After pushing FLAGS during interrupt entry, which flags does the 8086 clear before starting the ISR?
questions.explanation: Clearing IF blocks further INTR requests, and clearing TF stops single-stepping inside the ISR. IRET restores both from the saved FLAGS.

questions.questionText: When several interrupts are pending at the same time, which of these has the lowest priority in the 8086?
questions.explanation: The 8086 priority is: divide error, INT n and INTO highest, then NMI, then INTR, and single step lowest. Single step is therefore the last one the CPU recognises when several requests are pending together.

questions.questionText: The 8086 has no instruction that sets TF directly. A program uses PUSHF, POP AX, OR AX,x, PUSH AX, POPF. What is x?
questions.explanation: TF is bit 8 of the FLAGS register, so x = 2^8 = 0100H. 0200H would set IF (bit 9), 0080H SF (bit 7) and 0400H DF (bit 10).

questions.questionText: When the 8086 acknowledges an INTR request from an 8259, the type number is placed on the data bus during:
options: Both INTA cycles, one nibble each
The memory read of the IVT entry
questions.explanation: The first INTA cycle tells the 8259 to freeze and resolve the request; during the second INTA cycle the 8259 drives the 8-bit type onto D0-D7.

questions.questionText: An 8259 in an 8086 system is used alone (no cascading), with edge-triggered inputs, and ICW4 will be sent. The ICW1 byte is:
questions.explanation: ICW1 = A7 A6 A5 1 LTIM ADI SNGL IC4 = 0001 0011 = 13H (D4 = 1 identifies ICW1, LTIM = 0 edge, SNGL = 1, IC4 = 1). 1BH selects level triggering, 11H cascade mode and 03H omits D4.

questions.questionText: An 8259 in 8086 mode has been given ICW2 = 70H. Which interrupt type is generated for a request on IR5?
questions.explanation: The 8259 supplies T7-T3 from ICW2 and the IR number in the low three bits: 70H + 5 = 75H. 1D4H is the vector address of that type (75H × 4), not the type.

questions.questionText: A master 8259 has slave 8259s connected to its IR1 and IR6 inputs. The ICW3 byte sent to the master is:
questions.explanation: In the master ICW3 each bit marks an IR input that has a slave: D6 = 1 and D1 = 1 gives 0100 0010 = 42H. BDH is the complement, and 16H/61H just write the IR numbers as digits.

questions.questionText: A slave 8259 is connected to the IR6 input of the master. The ICW3 byte sent to this slave is:
questions.explanation: A slave ICW3 holds its ID in D2-D0, equal to the master IR input it is wired to: 6 = 0000 0110 = 06H. 40H is the bit-mask form, which is used only for the master.

questions.questionText: The ICW4 byte for an 8259 in an 8086 system with normal EOI, non-buffered operation and no special fully nested mode is:
questions.explanation: ICW4 = 0 0 0 SFNM BUF M/S AEOI µPM. Only µPM = 1 (8086/8088 mode) is set: 0000 0001 = 01H. 00H selects 8085 mode, 03H adds automatic EOI and 11H adds special fully nested mode.

questions.questionText: Using OCW1, an 8259 must accept requests only on IR0, IR1 and IR4. The byte written to the mask register is:
questions.explanation: A 1 in the IMR masks an input, so every bit except D0, D1 and D4 must be 1: 1110 1100 = ECH. 13H is the inverse (it would enable all the others).

questions.questionText: The OCW2 byte for a specific End of Interrupt for IR5 is:
questions.explanation: Specific EOI: R = 0, SL = 1, EOI = 1 and L2-L0 = 101: 0110 0101 = 65H. 25H lacks SL (so it is treated as non-specific), and E5H also rotates priority.

questions.questionText: Which byte, written to the 8259 with A0 = 0, makes the next read return the In-Service Register?
questions.explanation: OCW3 = 0 ESMM SMM 0 1 P RR RIS; RR = 1, RIS = 1 selects the ISR: 0000 1011 = 0BH. 0AH selects IRR, 0CH is a poll command and 03H has D3 = 0, so it would be taken as an OCW2.

questions.questionText: ICW1, OCW2 and OCW3 are all written to the 8259 with A0 = 0. How does the 8259 tell them apart?
options: By the order of writing only: the first A0 = 0 byte is always ICW1, later ones alternate OCW2 and OCW3
D7 = 1 means ICW1; D7 = 0 means an OCW
D4 = 1 means ICW1; with D4 = 0, D3 = 0 means OCW2 and D3 = 1 means OCW3
D0 = 1 means ICW1; D0 = 0 means OCW2 or OCW3
questions.explanation: ICW1 always has D4 = 1 and starts the initialisation sequence. OCW2 and OCW3 both have D4 = 0 and are distinguished by D3.

questions.questionText: An 8259 is in automatic rotation mode. IR3 has just been serviced and received its EOI. Which input now has the highest priority?
questions.explanation: With rotation, the level just served becomes the lowest, so the order becomes IR4, IR5, IR6, IR7, IR0, IR1, IR2, IR3 and IR4 is highest.

questions.questionText: A master 8259 has slave 8259s on three of its IR inputs and nothing else is cascaded. What is the maximum number of interrupt request inputs available?
questions.explanation: Each slave takes over one master input: (8 − 3) master inputs + 3 × 8 slave inputs = 5 + 24 = 29. Counting 8 per chip gives 32, which double-counts the three master inputs.

questions.questionText: In a cascaded 8259 system, the CAS0-CAS2 lines are used to:
options: Carry the 8-bit interrupt type from the slave to the CPU
Connect the INT outputs of the slaves to the INTR pin of the CPU
Let the master send the 3-bit ID of the slave that must place its type number on the bus
Select between ICW and OCW writes
questions.explanation: CAS0-CAS2 are outputs on the master and inputs on the slaves. During INTA the master puts the ID of the interrupting slave on them (3 bits, so up to 8 slaves), and only that slave responds.

questions.questionText: What is the effect of programming the 8259 in automatic EOI (AEOI) mode?
options: The ISR bit is cleared when the CPU executes IRET
The IRR bit is never cleared, so the request repeats until masked
The ISR bit is cleared automatically at the end of the last INTA pulse, so the service routine sends no EOI command
All requests are masked until the CPU sends an EOI
questions.explanation: In AEOI mode the 8259 performs a non-specific EOI itself on the trailing edge of the last INTA pulse. The 8259 cannot see IRET, and the price is that it no longer protects a running ISR from lower-priority requests.

questions.questionText: Why is the master 8259 in a cascaded system programmed in special fully nested mode (SFNM)?
options: So that a higher-priority request from a slave that is already in service can still reach the CPU
So that the master can use CAS0-CAS2 as extra IR inputs
So that priorities rotate automatically among the slaves
So that the slaves do not need an EOI command
questions.explanation: In normal nested mode the master blocks every new request on an IR line whose ISR bit is set. With SFNM the master still passes a higher-priority request arriving from the same slave, keeping true priority inside that slave.

questions.questionText: When an 8259 is used in 8085 mode, how many INTA pulses does it need to deliver the interrupt response?
questions.explanation: In 8085 mode the 8259 supplies a CALL opcode (CDH) on the first INTA and the two address bytes on the next two INTA pulses. In 8086 mode it needs only two INTA pulses and supplies a type number.

questions.questionText: An 8259 in fully nested mode (normal EOI) services IR2, but the ISR returns with IRET without sending any EOI. What happens afterwards?
options: All eight inputs are blocked until the next reset
Requests on IR2 to IR7 are no longer passed to the CPU, but IR0 and IR1 still are
Nothing, because IRET clears the ISR bit automatically
Only IR2 is blocked; IR3 to IR7 still work normally
questions.explanation: The IR2 bit stays set in the In-Service Register, so the priority resolver holds off every request of equal or lower priority (IR2-IR7). Higher-priority IR0 and IR1 can still interrupt.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is serviced by the 8086 without any INTA bus cycles, because its type number is fixed?
options: A rising edge on the NMI pin
An INTR request from a single 8259
An INTR request from a slave 8259 in cascade
An INTR request from a device that supplies type 40H
questions.explanation: NMI is always type 2, so the CPU goes straight to vector 00008H. Every INTR request, whatever its source, needs the two INTA cycles to read the type number.

questions.questionText: Memory locations 00020H-00023H of an 8086 system contain 23H, 45H, 00H, C8H (in increasing address order). At what physical address does the ISR for INT 08H begin?
questions.explanation: IP = word at 00020H = 4523H, CS = word at 00022H = C800H. Physical address = C800H × 16 + 4523H = C8000H + 4523H = CC523H.

questions.questionText: An 8086 has SS = 3000H and SP = 0200H when it accepts an interrupt. At which physical address is the low byte of the saved IP stored?
questions.explanation: FLAGS go to SS:01FEH, CS to SS:01FCH and IP to SS:01FAH (SP ends at 01FAH). Physical = 3000H × 16 + 01FAH = 301FAH. 031FAH forgets to multiply SS by 16.

questions.questionText: An 8086 executes MOV AX,0400H; MOV BL,02H; DIV BL. What happens?
options: AL = 00H and AH = 02H, with no interrupt
A type 0 (divide error) interrupt occurs, because the quotient does not fit in AL
questions.explanation: DIV BL divides AX by BL and must put the quotient in AL. 0400H / 02H = 0200H, which exceeds FFH, so the 8086 raises a type 0 interrupt through vector 00000H.

questions.questionText: An 8086 executes MOV AL,7FH; ADD AL,01H; INTO. What happens at INTO?
options: A type 4 interrupt, using the vector at 00010H
Nothing, because CF = 0 after the addition
A type 4 interrupt, using the vector at 00004H
A type 0 interrupt, using the vector at 00000H
questions.explanation: 7FH + 01H = 80H: two positive signed bytes give a negative result, so OF = 1 (CF = 0). INTO therefore calls type 4, whose vector is at 4 × 4 = 00010H.

questions.questionText: An 8259 in 8086 mode is initialised with ICW2 = 40H. When IR3 is requested, the 8086 reads the ISR address from the IVT entry starting at:
questions.explanation: Type = 40H + 3 = 43H. Vector address = 4 × 43H = 0010CH. 00043H forgets the × 4, 00430H multiplies by 16, and 0004CH adds 3 × 4 to 40H.

questions.questionText: The 8259 receives the command C5H with A0 = 0. Which IR input now has the highest priority?
questions.explanation: C5H = 1100 0101: D4 = 0 and D3 = 0, so it is OCW2; R = 1, SL = 1, EOI = 0 is the set-priority command with L = 5 as the lowest. The order becomes IR6, IR7, IR0, ..., IR5, so IR6 is highest.

questions.questionText: An 8086 system needs 16 separate hardware interrupt inputs using 8259A controllers. What is the minimum number of 8259A chips?
questions.explanation: One master + 1 slave gives only 7 + 8 = 15 inputs, because the slave occupies one master input. With 2 slaves: 6 + 16 = 22 ≥ 16, so 3 chips are needed.

questions.questionText: A program installs the ISR for INT 60H at 2000H:0100H by writing the IVT directly. Which address and bytes (in increasing address order) are correct?
questions.explanation: Entry = 4 × 60H = 180H = 00180H. IP = 0100H is stored low byte first (00 01), then CS = 2000H (00 20), giving 00 01 00 20.

questions.questionText: An 8086 writes 0CH to its 8259 with A0 = 0 and then reads the 8259, obtaining 85H. What does this tell the program?
options: IR0 and IR2 are requesting service
No interrupt is pending, because bit D3 is 0
An interrupt is pending and IR5 is the highest-priority request
questions.explanation: 0CH = 0000 1100 is OCW3 with P = 1, a poll command. The poll word read back has D7 = I (1 = request pending) and D2-D0 = the highest-priority level: 85H = 1000 0101, so IR5.
